topics.intro: Temperature tells us how hot something is. You will learn the Celsius, Fahrenheit, Kelvin and Rankine scales, how to convert between them, and how thermometers are defined.

sections.title: Temperature scales and absolute zero
body: **Temperature** tells how hot or cold something is. It is measured in degrees on several scales. **Celsius (°C):** water freezes at 0° and boils at 100°. **Fahrenheit (°F):** water freezes at 32° and boils at 212°. **Kelvin (K):** the SI scale. It starts at **absolute zero**, where molecules have the least possible energy.

**Conversions.** **K = °C + 273.15** (many questions use 273). **T_F = 1.8 T_C + 32**, which is the same as T_F = (9/5)T_C + 32. And **T_C = (T_F − 32)/1.8**, which is about 0.556(T_F − 32) = 0.556 T_F − 17.78. Body temperature 37 °C is 1.8 × 37 + 32 = 98.6 °F and 310.15 K.

**Hydrogen example.** It freezes at −259.4 °C and boils at −252.9 °C. In kelvin (using 273): −259.4 + 273 = **13.6 K** and −252.9 + 273 = **20.1 K.** (Kelvin has no negative values and never uses the degree sign.)

**The Rankine scale** uses the Fahrenheit size of degree but starts at absolute zero: **°R = °F + 459.67**, and **R = 1.8 K.** So a Rankine reading is 1.8 times the Kelvin reading. The two readings can only be numerically equal at **0**, which is absolute zero. Absolute zero is −273.15 °C, which is −459.67 °F, and 0 K and 0 °R.

**Which temperature is the highest?** Convert everything to one scale. 100 K = −173 °C. 200 °R = 111.1 K = −162 °C. −13 °F = (−13 − 32)/1.8 = −25 °C. −32 °C stays as it is. The highest of these is −25 °C, which is **−13 °F.** (A common mistake is to compare the numbers directly.)

**A formula that is NOT correct** is one that mixes units. 'T_F = −460 °C' is nonsense because it labels a Fahrenheit value with °C. A correct statement is that absolute zero is −460 °F (about −459.67 °F).
keyPoints: Convert all values to one scale before comparing.
Rankine = 1.8 × Kelvin, so they agree only at absolute zero.

sections.title: The zeroth law and measuring temperature
body: **The zeroth law of thermodynamics:** if A is in thermal equilibrium with C, and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This is the basis of the **concept of temperature.** It is why a thermometer (C) can tell you whether two bodies have the same temperature.
**Thermometers** use a property that changes steadily with temperature: the length of a liquid column, the resistance of a wire, the pressure of a gas, and so on.

**The triple point of water** is fixed at **273.16 K** by definition. A **resistance thermometer** reads T = 273.16 × (R/R_tp), if its resistance rises in proportion to T. With R_tp = 90.95 Ω, a reading of R = 96.28 Ω gives T = 273.16 × 96.28/90.95 = **289.17 K.**

**Why mercury is used in thermometers.** It is easily visible (shiny), it expands almost **uniformly** over a wide range, and it does **not wet** glass, so the thread does not stick. Being a good conductor of heat is useful too (quick response), but the usual three listed properties are: visible, uniform expansion, not wetting glass.
keyPoints: Zeroth law: equilibrium with a third body means equal temperature.
Triple point of water = 273.16 K.
Resistance thermometer: T = 273.16 R/R_tp.

topics.intro: Heat is energy flowing because of a temperature difference. You will use Q = mcΔT, solve mixing problems, find specific heat capacity from an electric heater, and work with latent heat and ice.

sections.title: Heat, specific heat capacity and mixing
body: **Heat** is energy moving because of a temperature difference. The heat needed to change the temperature of a mass m is **Q = mcΔT**, where c is the **specific heat capacity** (the heat to warm 1 kg by 1 K). Water has c = 4200 J/kg·K. 1 kilocalorie = 4186 J.
**Same heat, equal masses.** Equal masses of copper and aluminium get the same heat Q. Their specific heats differ, so their temperature rises ΔT = Q/(mc) differ. Only Q is the same.

**Mixing (the heat lost by the hot water equals the heat gained by the cold).** Mixing masses of the same liquid, the final temperature is the **mass-weighted average:** T_f = (m₁T₁ + m₂T₂)/(m₁ + m₂). A bath has 70 kg at 26 °C and 10 kg at 90 °C is poured in: T_f = (70 × 26 + 10 × 90)/80 = 2720/80 = **34 °C.**
**Another.** 100 kg at 30 °C plus 20 kg at 80 °C: T_f = (3000 + 1600)/120 = **38.33 °C.** Give the exact value, since 38.33 is not 38.7.
**Power and energy.** Power is energy per second, so Q = Pt. A machine wasting 250 W for 5 s wastes 1250 J, which is 1250/4186 = **0.299 kcal.**

**Measuring c with a heater.** A 60 W heater warms an 80 g block for 5 min (300 s) and the temperature rises by 20 °C. Q = 60 × 300 = 18,000 J. c = Q/(mΔT) = 18,000/(0.08 × 20) = **11,250 J/kg·K** (11.25 kJ/kg·K).
keyPoints: Q = mcΔT; Q = Pt; 1 kcal = 4186 J.
Mixing the same liquid: mass-weighted average temperature.
Heat lost = heat gained.

sections.title: Latent heat and energy conversions
body: **Latent heat** is the heat needed to change the **state** (solid, liquid, gas) without changing the temperature. **Q = mL.** For ice melting, L_f = 334,000 J/kg. For water boiling, L_v = 2,265,000 J/kg (about 2.26 MJ/kg).

**Ice melted by hot water.** 80 g of water at 30 °C is poured on a large block of ice at 0 °C. The water cools to 0 °C and gives out Q = mcΔT = 0.08 × 4200 × 30 = 10,080 J. This melts a mass m = Q/L = 10,080/334,000 = 0.0302 kg = **30.2 g** of ice. (The ice stays at 0 °C, so all of the heat goes to melting.)

**Mechanical energy turning into heat.** If a falling mass gives all its potential energy mgh as heat, then mgh = mcΔT, so ΔT = gh/c. The mass cancels. A waterfall of height 840 m where the water keeps 50% of the energy: ΔT = 0.5 × 9.8 × 840/4200 = **0.98 °C.**

**A stopping object.** A 2 kg block moving at 10 m/s stops completely and all its kinetic energy becomes heat: ½mv² = 100 J. If this heats 1 kg of water, ΔT = 100/4200 = 0.024 °C. Very small, because the specific heat of water is large.
keyPoints: Q = mL for a change of state.
Falling energy to heat: ΔT = gh/c.
The ice stays at 0 °C while melting.

topics.intro: Things get bigger when heated. You will calculate how much a rod, a beam or a slab grows, how area, volume and density change, and how pressure compresses a liquid.

sections.title: Linear, area and volume expansion
body: Most solids get bigger when heated. A rod of length L that is heated by ΔT expands by **ΔL = αLΔT**, where **α** is the **coefficient of linear expansion** (per °C). A 10 m concrete slab heated from −10 °C to 35 °C (ΔT = 45 °C), with α = 1 × 10⁻⁵ per °C, grows by 10 × 10⁻⁵ × 45 = **0.0045 m** (4.5 mm). Notice that ΔT is the **change** in temperature.
A beam 15.0 m long heated through 40 °C with α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C: ΔL = 15 × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 40 = 7.2 × 10⁻³ m = **7.2 mm.**

**Area and volume.** For a thin sheet, the area increases by about **2α** per degree, and for a solid the volume increases by about **3α.** If a rod's cross-section has initial area A₀, the final area is **A = A₀(1 + 2αθ)**, so the ratio of final to initial area is **1 + 2αθ.**

**Density falls when heated.** The mass stays the same while the volume rises, so **ρ = ρ₀/(1 + 3αΔT).** Brass has density 18.2 g/cm³ at 0 °C and α = 1.9 × 10⁻⁵ per °C. At 70 °C, 3αΔT = 3 × 1.9 × 10⁻⁵ × 70 = 0.00399, so ρ = 18.2/1.00399 = **18.13 g/cm³,** which is about 18.1 g/cm³.
keyPoints: ΔL = αLΔT; area expands 2α; volume 3α.
Density: ρ = ρ₀/(1 + 3αΔT).
ΔT is the change in temperature.

sections.title: Squeezing liquids: the bulk modulus
body: A liquid or a solid also changes volume when the pressure changes. The **bulk modulus K** measures how hard it is to compress something: **K = −ΔP/(ΔV/V)**, or in size only **ΔP = K × (ΔV/V).** The unit is N/m² (pascal).

**Example.** By how much must the pressure on a litre of water be raised to reduce its volume by 50%? With K = 2.25 × 10⁹ N/m², ΔV/V = 0.5 and ΔP = 2.25 × 10⁹ × 0.5 = **1.125 × 10⁹ N/m²,** about 1.1 × 10⁹ N/m².
The large number shows how **incompressible** water is. Its volume falls by only 0.05% when the pressure increases by 10⁶ Pa (about 10 atmospheres), since ΔV/V = ΔP/K = 10⁶/2.25 × 10⁹ = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴.
A compressed liquid has more internal energy but the change in volume is tiny. This is why liquids are used in hydraulic machines to transmit force.
keyPoints: ΔP = K(ΔV/V).
A large K means hard to compress.
Water is nearly incompressible.

topics.intro: Heat travels by conduction, convection and radiation. You will learn the formula for each, solve window and radiator problems, and see why the temperature must be in kelvin for radiation.

sections.title: Conduction and convection
body: Heat moves in three ways: **conduction, convection and radiation.** Only **radiation does not need a material medium**, because it travels as electromagnetic waves and can cross a vacuum (that is how the Sun's heat reaches us).

**Conduction** is the passing of heat through a solid by neighbouring particles, with no bulk movement. The rate of heat flow through a slab is **H = kA(ΔT)/L**, where k is the thermal conductivity (W/m·K), A is the area, L is the thickness and ΔT is the temperature difference across it.

**Window example.** A room at 25 °C, outside at 0 °C, glass of area 2 m², thickness 2 mm = 0.002 m, k = 1 W/m·°C. H = (1 × 2 × 25)/0.002 = **25,000 W = 2.5 × 10⁴ W.** Always change millimetres into metres first.

**Convection** is heat carried by the **movement of a fluid** (liquid or gas). It happens because heating makes a fluid expand, so it becomes **less dense and rises**, while cooler, denser fluid sinks. The result is a circulating current. Hot air rising above a heater is an example.

**Newton's law of cooling:** the rate of heat loss by convection is **H = hAΔT.** The convection coefficient **h** depends on the fluid's **velocity**, the **nature of the fluid** (its properties) and the **nature of the surface.** It does not depend on any 'fluid acceleration'.
**Heat from an electric current** passing through a resistance (Joule heating) is an **irreversible** process. It always increases the entropy of the universe and cannot run in reverse by itself.
keyPoints: H = kAΔT/L (conduction); H = hAΔT (convection).
Only radiation needs no medium.
Convection: warm fluid rises because it is less dense.

sections.title: Thermal radiation
body: Every body gives out electromagnetic radiation. The power radiated by a surface is given by the **Stefan–Boltzmann law:** **P = eσAT⁴**, where **T is in kelvin**, A is the area, **σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²K⁴** and **e** is the emissivity (1 for a perfect 'black body', less than 1 for others).
The fourth power matters a lot: doubling the kelvin temperature raises the power by 2⁴ = **16 times.**

**Net radiation.** A body at temperature T in surroundings at T₀ both radiates and absorbs. The **net** power lost is **P_net = eσA(T⁴ − T₀⁴).** For a radiator with e = 0.7, A = 1.5 m², at 100 °C (373.15 K) in a room at 20 °C (293.15 K): P = 0.7 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 1.5 × (293.15⁴ − 373.15⁴). Taking the difference in the order 'surroundings minus radiator' gives a negative number, **−7.1 × 10² W** (about −714 W): the radiator **loses** heat, and the minus sign shows the direction.

**Finding an area.** A 100 W lamp has a tungsten filament at 3540 K with e = 0.50. A = P/(eσT⁴) = 100/(0.5 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 3540⁴) = **2.25 × 10⁻⁵ m².** The very small area is why the filament is a thin coil.
**Always convert °C to kelvin** before using T⁴. Using Celsius values gives wrong answers.
keyPoints: P = eσAT⁴, T in kelvin.
Net: eσA(T⁴ − T₀⁴).
Doubling T gives 16 times the power.

topics.intro: This topic explains gases through the motion of their molecules. You will use the ideal gas law, find molecular energies and degrees of freedom, and compare molecular speeds as the temperature changes.

sections.title: The ideal gas law and the gas constant
body: The **ideal gas law:** **PV = nRT**, where P is the pressure (Pa), V the volume (m³), n the number of moles, T the temperature in **kelvin**, and **R = 8.314 J/mol·K.** Always change litres or cm³ to m³ first (1 L = 10⁻³ m³ and 1000 cm³ = 10⁻³ m³).
**Number of moles.** An ideal gas in a 1000 cm³ container at 20 °C has pressure 1.00 × 10⁵ N/m². n = PV/(RT) = (10⁵ × 10⁻³)/(8.314 × 293.15) = 100/2437.3 = **0.0410 mol** (4.11 × 10⁻² mol).

**The gas constant per unit mass** (the specific gas constant) is **R_specific = R/M**, where M is the molar mass in **kg/mol.** For hydrogen, M = 2.016 g/mol = 0.002016 kg/mol, so R_specific = 8.314/0.002016 = **4.12 × 10³ J/kg·K** (the closest option is 4.13 × 10³).
**The molar heat capacities** of an ideal gas: C_p − C_v = R, and per kilogram, c_p − c_v = R/M. So the specific heat at constant volume is c_v = c_p − R/M.
**Viscosity** is a fluid's resistance to flow. From η = F L/(A v), its dimensions are (MLT⁻²)(L)/((L²)(LT⁻¹)) = **ML⁻¹T⁻¹.**
keyPoints: PV = nRT with T in kelvin and V in m³.
Specific gas constant = R/M (M in kg/mol).
Viscosity: ML⁻¹T⁻¹.

sections.title: Molecular energy and degrees of freedom
body: **Kinetic theory assumptions.** (1) A gas has a huge number of molecules moving randomly at many speeds. (2) The molecules are far apart on average, and their size is tiny compared with the distances between them. (3) The molecules **do not interact** except in brief collisions, so between collisions they move freely. (4) Collisions with each other and with the walls are **perfectly elastic.** A statement saying that the molecules interact during ordinary motion, or that collisions are perfectly inelastic, breaks these assumptions.

**Average kinetic energy** of one molecule's translation is **(3/2)kT**, where k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K is the Boltzmann constant. At 37 °C = 310.15 K it is 1.5 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 310.15 = **6.42 × 10⁻²¹ J.**

**Degrees of freedom** are the independent ways a molecule can store energy. A monatomic gas (like helium) has **3** (translation). A diatomic gas (like N₂ or O₂) has **5** (3 translation and 2 rotation) at ordinary temperatures. Each degree of freedom holds (1/2)kT per molecule, or (1/2)RT per mole.

**Internal energy of n moles:** monatomic **U = (3/2)nRT**, diatomic **U = (5/2)nRT.** At the same temperature, U_diatomic/U_monatomic = 5/3. If a mole of monatomic gas has 3.7 × 10⁴ J, a mole of diatomic gas at the same temperature has 3.7 × 10⁴ × 5/3 = **6.17 × 10⁴ J** (6.2 × 10⁴ J).
**Common mistakes.** Diatomic molecules have 5 degrees of freedom, not 6. And the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature.
keyPoints: Average KE per molecule = (3/2)kT.
Monatomic: 3 degrees of freedom; diatomic: 5.
U = (3/2)nRT (monatomic); U = (5/2)nRT (diatomic).

sections.title: Speeds of molecules
body: The **root-mean-square speed** is **v_rms = √(3kT/m)** for one molecule of mass m, or **√(3RT/M)** using the molar mass M in kg/mol. It tells you how fast the molecules typically move. It depends on **temperature** and on the **mass** of the molecule.

**Temperature change.** v_rms ∝ √T, with T in **kelvin.** From 20 °C to 40 °C: √(313.15/293.15) = 1.0335, so the speed rises by about **3.4%** (the nearest of the options 1%, 2%, 3%, 4% is 3%). From 30 °C to 50 °C: √(323.15/303.15) = 1.0325, a rise of **3.2%.** Using Celsius values directly would be a serious error.
**Which is faster?** At the same temperature, lighter molecules move faster. At 300 K, √(3RT/M) is 1925 m/s for hydrogen (M = 0.002016) but only 483 m/s for oxygen (M = 0.032).
**Doubling the temperature (in kelvin)** raises v_rms by a factor of only √2 = 1.41. To double v_rms, you need four times the kelvin temperature.
**Comparing temperatures in different scales.** Convert all values to a single scale (see Part 1 of the temperature lesson) before deciding which is highest.
keyPoints: v_rms = √(3kT/m) = √(3RT/M).
v_rms ∝ √T (kelvin).

topics.intro: Thermodynamics deals with heat, work and energy. You will learn the first law, the main gas processes, how heat engines and the Carnot cycle work, and the meaning of the second law and entropy.

sections.title: The first law and the processes of a gas
body: **The first law of thermodynamics** is energy conservation for heat: **ΔU = Q − W.** ΔU is the change in the internal energy of the system, **Q is the heat added to** the system, and **W is the work done BY the system** on its surroundings. If work is done **on** the system, W is negative.

**Example.** 75 J of work is done on a system by stirring with a paddle wheel, while 63 J of heat is removed. The work done by the system is W = −75 J, and Q = −63 J (heat leaves). ΔU = Q − W = −63 − (−75) = **+12 J.** The system's energy rises by 12 J.

**Special processes.** **Isothermal** (constant temperature): ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, and **W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁).** One mole expanding at 310 K from 12 L to 19 L: W = 8.314 × 310 × ln(19/12) = 2577 × 0.4595 = **1184 J.** **Adiabatic** (no heat flow): **Q = 0**, so ΔU = −W. **Isobaric** (constant pressure): **W = P(V₂ − V₁).** **Isochoric** (constant volume): W = 0.

**Boiling water.** 1 kg of water at 100 °C becomes steam at 1 atm. The volume goes from 10⁻³ m³ to 1.671 m³. Heat absorbed Q = mL_v = 2265 kJ. Work done by the expansion W = PΔV = 1.01 × 10⁵ × 1.670 = 168.7 kJ. So ΔU = Q − W = 2265 − 168.7 = **2096 kJ.** Most of the heat raises the internal energy, since the molecules are being pulled apart.
**Which is the defining property of an adiabatic process?** It is dQ = 0. (The relation dU = −dW follows from it.)
keyPoints: ΔU = Q − W, with W the work done by the system.
Isothermal: W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁). Adiabatic: Q = 0.
Work done on the system counts as negative W.

sections.title: Heat engines and the Carnot cycle
body: A **heat engine** takes heat Q_h from a **hot source** at high temperature, turns some of it into **work W**, and rejects the rest, Q_c, to a **cold sink** at low temperature. So it works between a source, a sink and a working substance (the gas or steam doing the work). It cannot turn all the heat into work.
**Efficiency** η = W/Q_h = 1 − Q_c/Q_h. An engine that takes 500 J and does 200 J of work has η = 0.4 = 40%, and rejects 300 J.

**The Carnot cycle** is the ideal reversible engine. It has four stages: **isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression and adiabatic compression.** It has two isothermal and two adiabatic processes. It has **no isobaric stage.**

**Carnot's theorem:** all reversible engines working between the same two temperatures have the same efficiency, whatever the working substance, and no engine can do better. The efficiency is **η = 1 − T_c/T_h**, with temperatures in **kelvin.**
**Finding a temperature.** A Carnot engine with η = 75% has a sink at 300 K. Then 0.75 = 1 − 300/T_h, so T_h = 300/0.25 = **1200 K.**
**Finding the work.** A Carnot engine works between 227 °C (500 K) and 127 °C (400 K) and absorbs 6 × 10⁵ J. η = 1 − 400/500 = 0.2, so W = 0.2 × 6 × 10⁵ = **1.2 × 10⁵ J.**

**Power.** A reversible engine works between 527 °C (800 K) and 127 °C (400 K). Its efficiency is 1 − 400/800 = 0.5. To give 750 W of useful work it must take in 750/0.5 = 1500 W. With 1 W = 0.239 cal/s, that is 1500 × 0.239 = **358.5 cal/s.**

**Relative efficiency.** The reservoirs are at 600 K and 200 K, so the Carnot efficiency is 1 − 200/600 = 66.7%. If the engine runs at a relative efficiency of 48% (actual ÷ Carnot), its actual efficiency is 0.48 × 66.7% = **32%.**
keyPoints: η = W/Q_h = 1 − Q_c/Q_h; Carnot: η = 1 − T_c/T_h (kelvin).
Carnot cycle: 2 isothermal and 2 adiabatic stages.
No engine can turn all the heat into work.

sections.title: The second law and entropy
body: **The second law of thermodynamics** has several equivalent statements. **Clausius:** heat does not flow by itself from a cold body to a hot one. **Kelvin–Planck:** no engine can take heat from one reservoir and turn it **all** into work. Both say that real processes have a preferred direction.

The law is **statistical:** it describes what is overwhelmingly probable for huge numbers of molecules. Heat flows from hot to cold because that arrangement of energy is overwhelmingly more likely, not because of an absolute rule on each molecule.

**Entropy S** measures disorder, or the number of ways energy can be arranged. When heat Q enters at temperature T (kelvin), **ΔS = Q/T.** Melting 1 kg of ice at 273.15 K takes 334,000 J, so ΔS = 334,000/273.15 = **1223 J/K.** For an isolated system, the total entropy never decreases.

**Reversible and irreversible.** A reversible process can be undone with no net change anywhere. Real processes (friction, Joule heating, heat flowing through a temperature difference, mixing) are **irreversible** and increase the total entropy.
**A refrigerator** is an engine run backwards. It uses work to move heat from a cold region to a hot one, as described in the Clausius statement. It is allowed, but only when work is put in.
keyPoints: Second law: heat flows from hot to cold by itself; no engine turns all heat into work.
ΔS = Q/T (kelvin).

topics.intro: Elasticity describes how solids stretch and spring back. This lesson covers stress, strain, Hooke's law, the different moduli, and the speed of a pulse on a stressed wire.

sections.title: Stress, strain and the elastic moduli
body: When you pull, push or twist a solid, it deforms. **Stress** is the force per unit area: **stress = F/A** (N/m² = Pa). **Strain** is the fractional change in size, so it has no units. For small stresses the solid returns to its original size when the force is removed. This is the **elastic** region, and the stress beyond which this fails is the **elastic limit.**
**Example.** A force of 5 N acts on an aluminium cube with sides 15 cm. The area is 0.15² = 0.0225 m². Stress = 5/0.0225 = **222.2 N/m².** (The mass of the cube is not needed.)

**Hooke's law.** Within the elastic limit, **stress ∝ strain**, and the ratio is the **modulus.** There are three kinds. **Young's modulus E** = tensile stress/tensile strain, for stretching. **Shear modulus** = shear stress/shear strain, for **resistance to shear deformation** (sliding layers, like pushing the top of a book sideways). **Bulk modulus K** = pressure/volume strain, for squeezing.

**Stretching a wire.** A 2 m steel wire with area 1 mm² (10⁻⁶ m²) carries a 100 N load. E = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa. Stress = 100/10⁻⁶ = 10⁸ Pa. Strain = 10⁸/(2 × 10¹¹) = 5 × 10⁻⁴. Extension = strain × length = 5 × 10⁻⁴ × 2 = **1 × 10⁻³ m = 1 mm.** In one formula, **ΔL = FL/(AE).**
keyPoints: Stress = F/A; strain has no units.
Young's, shear and bulk moduli; modulus = stress/strain.
ΔL = FL/(AE).

sections.title: Wave speed and the elastic limit
body: A transverse pulse on a stretched wire travels at **v = √(T/μ)**, where T is the tension and μ is the mass per unit length. If the wire has cross-section A and density ρ, then μ = ρA and the tension is T = stress × A. So **v = √(stress/ρ).**

**Example.** The elastic limit of a steel wire is 2.70 × 10⁹ Pa and the density of steel is 7.86 × 10³ kg/m³. The greatest stress is the elastic limit, so the **maximum wave speed** is v = √(2.70 × 10⁹/7.86 × 10³) = √(3.435 × 10⁵) = **586 m/s.**
**What this means.** If the wire is stressed further than the elastic limit it is permanently damaged, so a pulse faster than 586 m/s cannot be sent without exceeding it.
**Check the units.** Pa = N/m² = kg/(m·s²), so Pa divided by kg/m³ gives m²/s², and the square root is m/s ✓.
keyPoints: v = √(T/μ) = √(stress/ρ).
Maximum stress = elastic limit.

topics.intro: Liquids have special properties. You will learn about phases, wetting, surface tension, capillary rise, and viscosity, including why mercury is used in thermometers.

sections.title: Phases, cohesion, adhesion and surface tension
body: **Phases.** A substance can be solid, liquid or gas. Two phases can **coexist in equilibrium** along the boundary between them. Water and steam coexist at the boiling point (100 °C at 1 atmosphere), and ice and water coexist at the melting point (0 °C). All three together coexist only at the **triple point** of water (273.16 K).
**Cohesion** is the attraction between molecules of the **same** substance. **Adhesion** is the attraction between molecules of **different** substances (liquid to container wall).

**Wetting.** A liquid **wets** a surface and spreads on it when **adhesion is greater than cohesion.** Water on clean glass wets it. If cohesion is greater than adhesion, as for mercury on glass, the liquid does not wet the surface and forms beads.

**Surface tension** is the tendency of a liquid surface to behave like a stretched skin, a force per unit length (N/m). It comes from the unbalanced attraction on molecules at the surface, so it is the result of **both cohesive forces (inside the liquid) and adhesive forces (at the solid interface).**

**Capillary rise.** In a narrow tube of radius r, a wetting liquid rises to **h = 2T cos θ/(ρgr)** (with θ the contact angle). For water (T = 0.072 N/m, ρ = 1000 kg/m³) in a tube of radius 0.5 mm, with θ = 0: h = 2 × 0.072/(1000 × 9.8 × 0.0005) = **0.029 m = 2.9 cm.** A narrower tube gives a bigger rise.
**Mercury** has a large cohesion and does not wet glass, so in a narrow tube it is **pushed down** below the outside level. This is also why it is a good thermometer liquid.
keyPoints: Wetting: adhesion greater than cohesion.
Surface tension comes from cohesive and adhesive forces.
Capillary rise: h = 2T cos θ/(ρgr).

sections.title: Viscosity and the flow of liquids
body: **Viscosity** is a fluid's resistance to flow, the 'thickness' of the liquid. Honey is more viscous than water. It comes from the friction between layers of fluid sliding past each other.
**Newton's law of viscosity:** the force between layers is **F = ηA(v/L)**, where η is the **coefficient of viscosity.** From this, **η = FL/(Av)**, and its dimensions are **ML⁻¹T⁻¹** (unit: Pa·s).
**Temperature effect.** The viscosity of a **liquid falls** as it is heated (honey flows faster when warm), but the viscosity of a **gas rises** with temperature.

**Terminal velocity.** A small sphere falling through a liquid speeds up until the viscous drag balances its weight (minus the upthrust). It then falls at a constant speed. A more viscous liquid gives a lower terminal velocity.
keyPoints: F = ηA(v/L); η has dimensions ML⁻¹T⁻¹.
Liquids get less viscous when warm; gases more viscous.
Terminal velocity: drag balances weight.
